summary: This experimental memo defines Directed ARP, a way for hosts and routers to find the link-level address for an advertised next-hop IP address on a different IP network.

eli5.summary: Computers use ARP to ask who lives at an address. This paper lets them ask about addresses on other networks, so they can talk directly instead of going through extra stops.

questions: resolving next hop addresses on foreign ip networks
when multiple ip networks share same link
subtitle: Resolving addresses on foreign IP networks over shared physical links

tldr.problem: When multiple IP networks share the same physical link, routing protocols want to advertise routes to addresses on foreign IP networks. But a host on one network has no way to resolve an IP address from another network to its physical address.
tldr.mechanism: Directed ARP extends the normal Address Resolution Protocol by adding an ARP Helper Address field to routing table entries. When resolving a foreign address, the host sends an ARP request to the helper router, which can resolve the address and reply.
tldr.outcome: This enables routers to advertise next-hop addresses on different IP networks via ICMP Redirects and dynamic routing protocols like BGP and OSPF, allowing more efficient routing when multiple networks share a physical link.

today: RFC 1433 remains Experimental. It was designed for public data networks with multiple IP networks on shared physical links, a scenario less common today. Modern networks use VLANs and other layer-2 virtualization rather than overlaid IP networks.

sections.title: The Problem: Multiple IP Networks on One Link
sections.content:
Large public data networks often have multiple IP networks running over the same physical link layer network. A router with an interface to both networks could benefit by advertising that the networks are reachable through each other, but a host on one network cannot directly communicate with the other without first resolving IP addresses to physical addresses.

The issue is that address resolution procedures are set up independently for each IP network. On an Ethernet, a host might broadcast an ARP request, but on other networks like SMDS, each IP network has its own separate multicast group for ARP. A host that does not know the correct ARP address group has no way to discover it or resolve an address on the foreign network.
sections.eli5: When two networks share one physical cable, computers need to talk across networks. But the address-lookup system is separate for each network, so a computer does not know how to look up addresses on the other side.

sections.title: ARP Helper Address
sections.content:
Directed ARP adds one new concept to routing tables: an ARP Helper Address field associated with each route entry. This field holds the IP address of a router that can assist in resolving the next-hop address. When the next-hop is on a foreign IP network, the ARP Helper Address is set to the IP address of the router that advertised the route (since that router must know how to reach that network). If the next-hop address can be resolved locally, the ARP Helper Address is NULL.

The routing function passes three pieces of information to address resolution: the next-hop IP address to resolve, the physical interface to use, and the ARP Helper Address. The resolver then decides whether to use normal local address resolution or to ask the helper router.
sections.eli5: Each route entry remembers a helper router's address. When looking up an address on a foreign network, the computer asks that helper router instead of trying to broadcast a request.

sections.title: Address Resolution Procedures
sections.content:
When the resolver needs to translate an IP address to a physical address, it follows a sequence. First, it checks the address resolution table for a cached entry. If found, it returns immediately.

If not cached and the ARP Helper Address is NULL, it uses the normal local address resolution procedure. But if an ARP Helper Address is present, the resolver must first resolve the helper address itself (recursively cached), and then sends an ARP request to that helper. The helper receives the request and replies with the physical address of the foreign IP address. This exchange uses the normal ARP packet format defined in RFC 826 and is compatible with existing ARP implementations.
sections.eli5: First try the cache. If the address is local or cached, use that. Otherwise, ask the helper router by sending it a normal ARP request. The helper replies with the answer.

sections.title: Router Forwarding of ARP Requests
sections.content:
Routers that implement Directed ARP must also forward incoming ARP requests that are not for their own address. When a router receives an ARP request for an IP address that is not on the router itself, it can forward the request to a helper router if the target address matches an entry in the router's routing table.

Before forwarding, the router checks whether the target IP address is a next-hop in the routing table, or a destination reachable through the same interface. If the request passes filtering constraints (to prevent ARP floods and loops), the router either forwards it to the associated ARP Helper Address, or if local address resolution is ARP-based, forwards it to the broadcast address for that network.
sections.eli5: Routers forward ARP requests they receive, sending them to the right place. They use filters to stop floods and loops from happening.

sections.title: Integration with Routing Protocols
sections.content:
ICMP Redirects allow a router to tell a host about a better next-hop. With Directed ARP, a router can advertise a next-hop on a foreign IP network; the host uses Directed ARP to resolve it. The ARP Helper Address is set to the router that sent the redirect, since the host should already know how to reach that router.

Distance-vector routing protocols like BGP can also advertise foreign next-hops. The router receiving such an advertisement sets the ARP Helper Address to the router that sent the update. Link-state protocols like OSPF can indicate that a single physical link connects to multiple IP networks, allowing other routers to calculate that a foreign network is reachable directly through that link.
sections.eli5: When routers share routing information, they can say a network is reachable through an address on another network. Directed ARP makes that information actually usable.

sections.title: Robustness and Black-Hole Prevention
sections.content:
Using third-party next-hops learned from routing protocols introduces risk: if that router fails, traffic may enter a black hole. Hosts and routers mitigate this by detecting failures using upper-layer protocols like TCP or ICMP echo. Additionally, SMDS networks and other link layers may apply filters that prevent direct communication even though routing suggests it is possible.

A host or router can verify link-level connectivity with a next-hop router by sending an ICMP echo directly to the physical address of that router, not to its IP address. If the test fails, the host should remove the routing table entry. Routers must ensure that routing information they advertise reflects real, usable paths, standing behind the routes they offer.
sections.eli5: If a helper router fails, traffic might get stuck. To avoid this, computers test whether they can actually reach a router before using it, and they only advertise routes they believe work.
